events.description: Battle of Toulouse: Duke Odo of Aquitaine defeated an invading Umayyad Muslim army.
Treaty of Paris ended the Albigensian Crusade; Toulouse incorporated into the French royal domain.
The Black Death struck Toulouse, causing major demographic crisis.
Great Fire of Toulouse ravaged the city for fifteen days; Louis XI subsequently exempted the city from taxes for 100 years.
Massacre of Huguenots in Toulouse at the start of the French Wars of Religion; Protestant capitouls and merchants fled the city.
French Revolution; Toulouse lost its role as capital of Languedoc and its parlement was abolished.
Flood of the Garonne devastated more than 1,000 houses and killed 200 people; destroyed all bridges except the Pont-Neuf.

entries.notes: Tolosa as oppidum of the Volcae Tectosages, a Gaulish tribe, before Roman conquest.
Toulouse became a Roman military outpost in the 2nd century BC during the Roman conquest of southern Gaul.
Developed as Roman city in Gallia Narbonensis under Augustus and through the imperial period.
Toulouse was capital of the Visigothic Kingdom, which stretched from the Loire to Gibraltar.
After Frankish conquest following Battle of Vouillé 507; Toulouse came under Frankish control.
County of Toulouse emerged within the Carolingian sub-kingdom of Aquitaine.
After Carolingian partition; County of Toulouse within West Francia.
County of Toulouse nominally under the Kingdom of France; came under direct royal control after Albigensian Crusade (Treaty of Paris, 1229).
French Revolution 1789; Toulouse lost role as capital of Languedoc and became head of Haute-Garonne department.
Napoleonic Empire.
Bourbon Restoration after Napoleon's defeat.
July Revolution 1830.
Second Republic established 1848.
Second Empire under Napoleon III.
Third Republic after Franco-Prussian War.
Toulouse under Vichy regime during WWII.
Liberation of Toulouse 1944.

value.name: Provisional Government of the French Republic

entries.notes: Fourth Republic established 1946.
Fifth Republic established 1958; Toulouse remains a major city and since 2016 regional prefecture of Occitanie.
Volcae Tectosages, a Gaulish tribe, inhabited the area before Roman conquest.
Toulouse developed as a Roman city in Gallia Narbonensis; Roman material culture dominant.
Frankish cultural context from 507; Merovingian period closes c. 751. Visigothic culture preceded but Frankish culture followed conquest.
Gaulish spoken by the Volcae Tectosages; gradually replaced by Latin after Roman conquest.
Latin as official and administrative language of Roman Toulouse; continued through late antiquity.
Occitan (langue d'oc) the vernacular language of Toulouse and the region throughout the medieval period.
French administrative presence increased after Treaty of Paris 1229 incorporated Toulouse into royal France.
Occitan continued as a spoken language but gradually displaced by French from the late medieval period onward; still present as a regional language.
French became the administrative and eventually dominant language; Ordinance of Villers-Cotterêts 1539 mandated French in legal documents.
Gaulish/Celtic religious practices among the Volcae Tectosages prior to and during Roman period.
Roman state religion dominant during Roman period; Domitian placed Toulouse under patronage of Pallas Athena.
Early Christian presence; Saint Saturnin (Sernin) martyred in Toulouse c. 250 AD, traditionally first bishop.
Christianity became state religion of Roman Empire under Theodosius; Toulouse has been Catholic ever since. Catharism suppressed by 1321.
Catharism was significant in Toulouse and surrounding region; Council of Toulouse 1229 laid foundations for Inquisition to eradicate it; effectively suppressed by mid-13th century.

Huguenots were a significant minority; French Wars of Religion began 1562; Toulouse became ultra-Catholic stronghold; Edict of Fontainebleau 1685 revoked Edict of Nantes, driving out remaining Protestants.
Tolosa attested as an oppidum on hills before Roman development; the Garonne Valley was a trade hub since at least the Iron Age.
Roman military outpost and then developed as a Roman city in Gallia Narbonensis from 2nd century BC.
Grew significantly under Roman rule; capital of Visigothic Kingdom in 5th century.
Second parlement of France established 1443; major administrative and judicial centre.
Became regional prefecture of Occitanie in 2016.
Article states 'between 35,000 and 40,000 inhabitants' in 1335; midpoint used.
